usamts-2019-r1-01.prompt:
Partition the grid into $1$ by $1$ squares and $1$ by $2$ dominoes in either orientation, marking dominoes with a line connecting the two adjacent squares, and $1$ by $1$ squares with an asterisk ($\ast$). No two $1$ by $1$ squares can share a side. A *border* is a grid segment between two adjacent squares that contain dominoes of opposite orientations. All borders have been marked with thick lines in the grid.

There is a unique solution, but you do not need to prove that your answer is the only one possible. You merely need to find an answer that satisfies the constraints above. (Note: In any other USAMTS problem, you need to provide a full proof. Only in this problem is an answer without justification acceptable.)
usamts-2019-r1-01.answer:
The unique partition is
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \rightarrow & \leftarrow & \downarrow & \ast & \downarrow & \ast & \rightarrow & \leftarrow & \rightarrow & \leftarrow\\\hline \downarrow & \ast & \uparrow & \downarrow & \uparrow & \downarrow & \downarrow & \rightarrow & \leftarrow & \ast\\\hline \uparrow & \rightarrow & \leftarrow & \uparrow & \ast & \uparrow & \uparrow & \ast & \rightarrow & \leftarrow\\\hline \rightarrow & \leftarrow & \downarrow & \ast & \rightarrow & \leftarrow & \ast & \rightarrow & \leftarrow & \ast\\\hline \downarrow & \ast & \uparrow & \downarrow & \ast & \rightarrow & \leftarrow & \rightarrow & \leftarrow & \downarrow\\\hline \uparrow & \downarrow & \ast & \uparrow & \downarrow & \ast & \rightarrow & \leftarrow & \ast & \uparrow\\\hline \downarrow & \uparrow & \downarrow & \ast & \uparrow & \downarrow & \ast & \rightarrow & \leftarrow & \ast\\\hline \uparrow & \ast & \uparrow & \downarrow & \ast & \uparrow & \rightarrow & \leftarrow & \ast & \downarrow\\\hline \rightarrow & \leftarrow & \downarrow & \uparrow & \rightarrow & \leftarrow & \ast & \downarrow & \downarrow & \uparrow\\\hline \rightarrow & \leftarrow & \uparrow & \rightarrow & \leftarrow & \rightarrow & \leftarrow & \uparrow & \uparrow & \ast\\\hline\end{array}$$
($\ast$ = a $1\times1$ square; each arrow points to the other half of its domino, so $\rightarrow\ \leftarrow$ is a horizontal domino and $\downarrow$ above $\uparrow$ is a vertical domino.)

usamts-2019-r1-02.prompt: Let $x$, $y$, and $z$ be real numbers greater than $1$. Prove that if $x^y = y^z = z^x$, then $x = y = z$.
usamts-2019-r1-02.answer: Assume $x<y$ and use that $a^s$ increases in $a$ (for $s>0$) and in $s$ (for $a>1$): $x^y=y^z>x^z$ gives $y>z$, $x^y=z^x<z^y$ gives $x<z$, and $y^z=z^x<y^x$ gives $z<x$ — a contradiction. Similarly $x>y$ is impossible, so $x=y$, and then $x^x=x^z$ gives $z=x$.

usamts-2019-r1-03.prompt: Circle $\omega$ is inscribed in unit square $PLUM$, and points $I$ and $E$ lie on $\omega$ such that $U$, $I$, and $E$ are collinear. Find, with proof, the greatest possible area for $\triangle PIE$.

usamts-2019-r1-04.prompt:
A group of $100$ friends stands in a circle. Initially, one person has $2019$ mangos, and no one else has mangos. The friends split the mangos according to the following rules:

* *sharing:* to share, a friend passes two mangos to the left and one mango to the right.
* *eating:* the mangos must also be eaten and enjoyed. However, no friend wants to be selfish and eat too many mangos. Every time a person eats a mango, they must also pass another mango to the right.

A person may only *share* if they have at least three mangos, and they may only *eat* if they have at least two mangos. The friends continue sharing and eating, until so many mangos have been eaten that no one is able to share or eat anymore.

Show that there are exactly eight people stuck with mangos, which can no longer be shared or eaten.
usamts-2019-r1-04.answer: Number the people $0,\dots,99$ going right, starting with the person who has the mangos. Then $\sum 2^i m_i \pmod{2^{100}-1}$ is invariant under both moves. At the end every $m_i\in\{0,1\}$, so $\sum 2^i m_i = 2019 = 11111100011_2$, which has eight $1$'s.

usamts-2019-r1-05.prompt:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. For integers $a, b$ with $0 \le a, b \le n-1$, let $r_n(a, b)$ denote the remainder when $ab$ is divided by $n$. If $S_n$ denotes the sum of all $n^2$ remainders $r_n(a, b)$, prove that
$$\frac12 - \frac{1}{\sqrt n} \le \frac{S_n}{n^3} \le \frac12.$$
usamts-2019-r1-05.answer: For fixed $b$ with $d=\gcd(b,n)$, the remainders $r_n(a,b)$ run $d$ times through $0,d,\dots,n-d$, summing to $\frac{n(n-d)}2$. So $\frac{S_n}{n^3} = \frac12 - \frac{1}{2n^2}\sum_{b=1}^{n}\gcd(b,n)$, and $0<\sum\gcd(b,n) = \sum_{d\mid n} d\,\varphi(n/d) \le n\,\tau(n) \le 2n\sqrt n$.
